paras: The Screven County ambush and threatened lynching of 1900 began on August 11, 1900, near Sylvania, Georgia, when a white man, R. F. Herrington, struck a Black man, Stephen Sanders, with a whip, and a white party that went that night to arrest Sanders on a peace warrant was fired on from ambush. Herrington and Constable Milton Mears were killed and Capt. Jesse T. Wade was wounded; an armed white mob then hunted the Black men blamed, and six prisoners were moved to Savannah for fear of a lynching. National wire reports called it a "race feud" and told the start differently.

The shooting took place in northern Screven County near the Savannah River swamps, where, according to the Savannah Morning News correspondent, there were "only about twenty-five white families and a hundred negroes."

In the account Wade gave from an Augusta hospital on August 17, Herrington and George Daniels met Sanders on a narrow road, and Sanders "insolently demanded them to turn out of his way." Herrington hit Sanders with his whip, and Sanders ran, then returned for his mule and, by Wade's account, said, "I'll kill you to-night." On Wade's advice Herrington swore out a peace warrant, which a Savannah telegram said was given to Constable Mears.

About 8:30 that evening the four men drove to the house of Jesse Sanders, Stephen's father, to serve it. While they told the elder Sanders to give up his son, shots came from a plum thicket beside the house, about forty of them according to the telegram. Wade, shot three times, escaped; Herrington and Mears were found dead the next morning.

On August 12 an armed mob searched for the Black men while Sheriff W. B. Thompson's posse sought to arrest them and keep them from the mob. According to the Savannah Morning News, only "diplomacy, mingled with some small show of force" let the sheriff save the lives of three men arrested that day. Nine Black men were in the Sylvania jail by August 13, and others were said to have fled to South Carolina.

On August 23, at the county commissioners' direction, the sheriff moved six prisoners to the Savannah jail because of the "double possibility" of a lynching or a jail delivery. The paper said the six had confessed and named Matthew McKinney as leader; Black ministers had asked the sheriff to protect them. On August 29 Governor Candler offered rewards for six men still at large, among them Jesse Alexander, Stephen Alexander and McKinney. The coverage does not report a trial or what became of Stephen Sanders.

The first dispatch said "two negroes named Alexander" shot Herrington and Mears on the road after a buggy collision and that Wade fell "mortally wounded" at their house. That version ran on August 13 from New York to Houston and Birmingham, under headlines announcing a "race feud," a "race war" and, in Mississippi, a "race riot threatened."

The Savannah Morning News called the accused a "band of black assassins" while reporting the sheriff's protection of them, and Wade's statement, the only one to mention the whip, insisted there was "no race war" in Screven.

The only Black-press coverage found, in the Richmond Planet of August 18, ran the wire dispatch twice, once as news and once in an editorial. There the Planet said "the business of rushing into colored men's houses without authority" was being met "in the regular 'white man fashion,'" and that Black residents were "desperate" because "the government affords no protection." It asked "Who can blame them?" and paired the case with a Virginia family who fired on a white mob.

The wire had the Alexanders shooting the two men on the road, while the telegram, Wade and the August 24 report placed all three at Jesse Sanders's house in one ambush. The later accounts are fuller and agree, but they come from the white party and officers, as does the threat attributed to Sanders. The governor's reward named a Jesse and a Stephen Alexander, the same given names Wade used for the Sanders father and son, and the coverage does not reconcile the surnames.

reader.title: Screven County ambush and threatened lynching of 1900
bases: The anti-Black violence consists of Herrington's whip blow to Stephen Sanders (A12) and, after two white men were killed, an armed white mob's search for the Black men blamed, from which the sheriff said he saved three, and the removal of six prisoners to Savannah for fear of a lynching (A15): a threatened lynching.

The killing of Herrington and Mears and the arrests are reported independently by the Sylvania correspondent, a Savannah telegram and Wade (A1, A7, A12), but the roadside encounter is told two ways: a buggy collision with two men named Alexander in the first wire reports (A1, A2) and a whip blow to Stephen Sanders in Wade's account (A12), with the Savannah telegram mentioning only a 'difficulty' with Sanders (A7).

accounts.label: First wire report (Sylvania, Aug. 12)
accounts.gist: Herrington and Mears' buggy collided with that of two Black men named Alexander, who shot them dead after a quarrel; a posse under Wade was fired on at the Alexanders' house and Wade fell 'mortally wounded'.

accounts.label: Savannah telegram (Aug. 13)
accounts.gist: Herrington had a 'difficulty' with a man named Sanders, who threatened to kill him; a peace warrant was given to Constable Mears, and about forty shots from ambush at Jesse Sanders's house killed Herrington and Mears and wounded Wade.

accounts.label: Capt. Wade's account (Aug. 17)
accounts.gist: Stephen Sanders 'insolently' demanded the road, Herrington whipped him, Sanders threatened him, and the party serving the peace warrant was fired on from a plum thicket while talking to Jesse Sanders; Wade denied any race war.

accounts.label: Officers and Savannah Morning News (Aug. 24)
accounts.gist: An armed mob searched for the men on Aug. 12; the sheriff saved three; six prisoners, said to have confessed and named McKinney as leader, were moved to Savannah because of the 'double possibility' of lynching or jail delivery.

accounts.label: Richmond Planet editorial
accounts.gist: Reprinting the wire story, the Planet treated the shooting as Black residents meeting armed intrusion into their homes in kind because the government gave them no protection.

framing.detail: Northern and Southern papers carried the collision dispatch on Aug. 13-16 under headlines such as 'RACE FEUD BREAKS OUT IN GEORGIA', 'DOUBLE MURDER PRECIPITATES A RACE WAR IN GEORGIA' and 'RACE RIOT THREATENED'.

The Savannah Morning News called the killing murder 'in cold blood' and the accused a 'band of black assassins', while reporting the sheriff's protection of the prisoners from a mob and Wade's insistence that there was 'no race war'.
The Richmond Planet condemned the 'business of rushing into colored men's houses without authority' and defended Black residents who 'sell their lives as dearly as possible'.

record_check.record: R. F. Harrington struck Stephen Sanders ... with his whip
record_check.dossier: The whip blow was the prelude to a night peace-warrant arrest, an ambush that killed Herrington and Mears, a mob search, and the removal of six prisoners to Savannah for fear of lynching.
The whip blow rests on Wade's account alone, but the episode is reported independently by several papers and the account of the encounter is contested.

Stephen Sanders, struck with a whip by R. F. Herrington; the Black men sought by an armed mob, including six prisoners (Cleveland Herrington, Andrew Davis, Samuel Balden, Richard Sanders, William Hudson, Arnold Augustus) moved to Savannah for fear of lynching
Stephen Sanders: accused by the white party of 'insolently' demanding the road and threatening to kill Herrington (peace warrant). The arrested men: accused of the murder of Herrington and Mears.
R. F. (Fillmore) Herrington, white, struck Sanders; an armed white mob searched for the accused on Aug. 12
No lynching reported; no report of indictment or trial, or of Stephen Sanders's fate, found through September
